title: Setting Up Raspberry Pi
subtitle: OS installation, headless SSH setup, networking, and raspi-config
author: Kernal Team

whyItExists.problem: Raspberry Pi is a full Linux computer that must be set up before it can run any project code. First-time users often struggle with flashing SD cards, enabling SSH headlessly, finding the Pi's IP address, and configuring the system.
whyItExists.solution: Raspberry Pi Imager simplifies OS installation with built-in support for headless configuration: WiFi credentials, SSH key, and hostname can all be preconfigured before the first boot — no keyboard or monitor needed.
whyItExists.whenToUse: For any embedded project requiring a full Linux OS: web servers, Python-based sensor systems, databases, computer vision, media players, or edge AI.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: For simple, low-power, real-time control tasks — an Arduino or ESP32 is cheaper, starts instantly, and uses <1 W vs Raspberry Pi's 2.5–7 W.

explainModes.beginner: Setting up a Raspberry Pi is like setting up a mini PC, but without a screen or keyboard at first. You put the operating system on a micro-SD card, plug it into the Pi, and connect to it over WiFi using SSH — it's like a remote terminal into the Pi from your laptop.
explainModes.simple: Raspberry Pi OS is a Debian Linux distribution that boots from a micro-SD card. Use Raspberry Pi Imager to flash the OS with your WiFi credentials and SSH key pre-entered. Connect via `ssh pi@raspberrypi.local` from any computer on the same network.
explainModes.standard: Raspberry Pi Imager writes the compressed .img file to SD, then applies a firstrun.sh cloud-init-style configuration script. SSH daemon starts on first boot. mDNS (via avahi-daemon) resolves raspberrypi.local to the Pi's IP without needing to check your router.
explainModes.technical: The boot partition is FAT32 (accessible from any OS) containing config.txt, cmdline.txt, and overlays. Linux root filesystem is ext4. GPU, CPU, and peripheral configuration go in config.txt. SSH can be enabled by an empty /boot/ssh file (legacy method) or via cloud-init userdata.
explainModes.deepDive: Raspberry Pi 4 uses a 64-bit ARM Cortex-A72 (BCM2711). It supports USB boot (no SD card needed) via EEPROM bootloader update. Overclocking in config.txt: `arm_freq=2000` and `over_voltage=6` for Pi 4B. Enable hardware watchdog with `dtparam=watchdog=on` and configure systemd watchdog in /etc/systemd/system.conf.

content.text: Flashing the SD Card with Raspberry Pi Imager

Download Raspberry Pi Imager from raspberrypi.com. Insert a micro-SD card (8 GB minimum, Class 10 recommended). In Imager: Choose OS → Raspberry Pi OS (64-bit) Lite for headless, or Desktop for GUI. Click the gear icon ⚙ (or Ctrl+Shift+X) to open Advanced Options before writing.

content.code:
Raspberry Pi Imager — Advanced Options (Ctrl+Shift+X)
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
✅ Set hostname:          mypi.local
✅ Enable SSH:            Use password authentication
   Username:             pi
   Password:             [your secure password]
✅ Configure wireless LAN:
   SSID:                 YourNetwork
   Password:             YourWiFiPassword
   Country:              IN (India) / US / GB
✅ Set locale:
   Timezone:             Asia/Kolkata
   Keyboard layout:      gb

→ Click SAVE, then WRITE

content.text: After first boot (wait 60–90 seconds), connect from any computer on the same WiFi. The Pi is discoverable by hostname via mDNS — no need to find its IP address.

content.code:
# Connect to Pi by hostname (mDNS — works on same network)
ssh pi@mypi.local
# Enter your password when prompted

# If hostname doesn't resolve, find IP from your router admin,
# or use nmap to scan your network:
nmap -sn 192.168.1.0/24 | grep -i raspberry

# Once connected, check system info
uname -a                     # kernel version + architecture
vcgencmd measure_temp        # CPU temperature
free -h                      # memory usage
df -h                        # disk usage

# Keep the connection alive (add to ~/.ssh/config on client)
# Host raspberrypi.local
#   ServerAliveInterval 60

content.text: sudo raspi-config is a text-based menu for configuring the Pi. Essential settings to check on a new installation:

content.code:
sudo raspi-config
# Key options:
# 1. System Options → S5 Boot / Auto Login → Console (no desktop)
# 3. Interface Options → I2  → Enable SSH (if not already)
#                      → I4  → Enable I2C (for sensors)
#                      → I3  → Enable SPI
#                      → I6  → Enable Serial Port (disable login shell)
# 6. Advanced Options → A1  → Expand Filesystem (uses full SD card)
#                      → A3  → Memory Split → 16 (for headless: less GPU RAM)

# Update the system (do this once after first boot)
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
sudo apt install -y vim htop git python3-pip python3-venv

# Set a static IP (optional — useful for server projects)
sudo nano /etc/dhcpcd.conf
# Add at end:
# interface wlan0
# static ip_address=192.168.1.100/24
# static routers=192.168.1.1
# static domain_name_servers=1.1.1.1 8.8.8.8

content.title: Raspberry Pi vs Arduino for Embedded Projects

a.name: Raspberry Pi
a.useWhen: Need Linux OS, database, web server, computer vision, or complex networking

b.name: Arduino / ESP32
strengths: < 1 W typical, µA in deep sleep
b.useWhen: Real-time control, battery power, simple I/O, cost-sensitive production

content.text: For the most robust headless Pi setup, copy your SSH public key to the Pi immediately after first login: `ssh-copy-id pi@mypi.local`. Then disable password authentication in /etc/ssh/sshd_config (set PasswordAuthentication no) so only key-based login works — much more secure.

Never abruptly unplug a Raspberry Pi — it can corrupt the SD card filesystem, requiring a full reflash. Always shut down gracefully with `sudo shutdown -h now` or `sudo poweroff`. For projects that may lose power, use a UPS HAT or configure the Pi to use a read-only overlay filesystem.

questions.question: How do you enable SSH headlessly before first Pi boot using Raspberry Pi Imager?
options: Use the Advanced Options (gear icon) in Imager to enable SSH before writing the image
Boot the Pi, run raspi-config, and enable SSH from there
Create an empty file called 'ssh' in the root partition
questions.explanation: Modern Raspberry Pi Imager (v1.7+) has Advanced Options (Ctrl+Shift+X or gear icon) that lets you preconfigure SSH, WiFi, hostname, and locale before writing — the preferred method for headless setup.

questions.question: What command connects you to a Raspberry Pi by hostname over SSH?
questions.explanation: ssh pi@raspberrypi.local connects using SSH. The hostname.local format uses mDNS (Avahi) to resolve the Pi's IP automatically on the local network — no need to look up the IP.

questions.question: Why is abruptly unplugging a Raspberry Pi dangerous?
options: It can corrupt the ext4 filesystem on the SD card, requiring a reflash
questions.explanation: Raspberry Pi OS uses a journaling ext4 filesystem, but writes may be in-flight when power cuts. Abrupt power loss can corrupt the SD card, leaving the Pi unbootable. Always use `sudo shutdown -h now`.

faq.q: What operating system does Raspberry Pi use?
faq.a: Raspberry Pi OS (formerly Raspbian), based on Debian Linux. The 64-bit Bookworm version (Debian 12) is current as of 2024. You can also run Ubuntu Server 22.04/24.04, Arch Linux ARM, or Alpine Linux — all support ARM64.

faq.q: My Pi isn't showing up at raspberrypi.local. What's wrong?
faq.a: Common causes: (1) WiFi credentials wrong in Imager — reflash with correct SSID/password; (2) the Pi is on 5 GHz WiFi but Raspberry Pi 3/Zero only supports 2.4 GHz; (3) mDNS not supported on your router — use nmap to find the IP; (4) first boot takes 90 seconds — be patient.

faq.q: Can I run Raspberry Pi from a USB drive instead of SD card?
faq.a: Yes! Pi 4 supports USB boot natively after a one-time EEPROM update (rpi-eeprom-update). USB 3.0 SSD is much faster and more reliable than SD cards for intensive projects. Pi 5 also supports NVMe SSD via its PCIe slot.
